title: Creative Destruction: Barriers to Urban Growth and the Great Boston Fire of 1872
research_question: Do widespread, simultaneous reconstruction opportunities in dense urban areas generate economic gains through positive cross-property spillovers, and how large are the constraints that outdated durable buildings impose on urban growth? Specifically, does forced replacement of older buildings raise land values on affected plots and on nearby unaffected plots, capitalizing meaningful gains relative to the value of destroyed structures?
data_description: The authors construct a new plot-level panel from digitized City of Boston tax assessment records for 1867, 1869, 1871, 1872, 1873, 1882, and 1894, covering all plots in the area destroyed by the 1872 fire and surrounding downtown areas (44,543 plots pooled across years). For each plot-year, the data include assessed land value, building value, land area, street address, commercial occupants' industry and business capital, and residential occupants' personal property. Plots are geo-located using fire insurance maps (Sanborn 1867, 1873, 1883, 1895; Bromley 1883). Supplemental data include property sales from Boston's Registry of Deeds (used to validate assessed values), records of individual building fires from the Boston Fire Department (1866–1891, 109 major fires), and infrastructure data on road widths and water pipe diameters. Dollar values are deflated to 1872 dollars using the David-Solar CPI.
institutional_context: In November 1872, a fire spread through Boston's downtown business district, destroying 776 buildings and causing roughly $75 million in damages (about 11 percent of total Boston real estate and personal property value). The burned area was a densely developed commercial neighborhood adjacent to the central business district. Reconstruction occurred in an era preceding zoning regulations and strong building codes; rebuilding was managed largely by private landowners, funded partly by insurance payouts and capital inflows. The city undertook modest road widening and Post Office Square creation, but more ambitious infrastructure and building-code reforms were defeated by landowner opposition. Construction technology of the period limited building heights, so reconstruction primarily upgraded building quality rather than density. Boston had been growing rapidly prior to the fire, with real estate values rising about 4.8 percent annually in the preceding two decades, providing strong demand for upgraded structures.
